lines.text: The nightly job reads one terabyte of order events... from a fast local drive.
The team wants to read it... straight from object storage instead.
Before anyone runs it... what is the least time each way could take?
By the end, you'll compute both... and the least setting that could make them match.
Let's predict first.
One read from RAM takes about a hundred nanoseconds.
Object storage takes about a hundred milliseconds to send the first byte.
How many RAM reads fit into one object storage wait?

lines.text: About a million. A hundred milliseconds, divided by a hundred nanoseconds.
That's the gap between one second... and eleven and a half days.
On a straight axis, the RAM read would vanish. So every latency chart from here on is logarithmic... equal steps are equal multiples.
Inside the chip, latency is counted in clock cycles.
Intel says a Skylake server core needs four to six cycles for the first level cache. The second level needs fourteen. The third level needs fifty to seventy.
A well known paper from two thousand seven puts main memory at two hundred cycles or more.
At two gigahertz, a cycle is half a nanosecond. So L one is two to three nanoseconds... and D RAM, about a hundred.

lines.text: Off the chip, the waits jump to microseconds, and then milliseconds.
A random read of four kilobytes from a fast server drive takes eighty microseconds, says Samsung's datasheet.
A hard disk waits for the platter to spin around... Seagate says four point one six milliseconds on average, at seven thousand two hundred turns a minute.
That drive did one hundred sixty eight random reads a second, measured with sixteen reads queued. So each read takes at least six milliseconds.
Object storage... a hundred to two hundred milliseconds to the first byte. Medians for small requests are in the tens of milliseconds.
The five hundred microsecond round trip is from two thousand nine. Amazon shows a live median in its network console, but no fixed number. Read yours, or measure.

of the processor that first touches it.

can leave its memory behind.

lines.text: Latency is how long until the first byte.
Bandwidth is how fast the bytes come after that.
They rank the tiers differently. RAM alone runs from twelve billion bytes a second on one core... to four hundred sixty point eight billion on one twelve channel socket, a peak from the spec sheet.
Object storage is the slowest rung to answer... yet Amazon says one machine can pull up to a hundred gigabits per second from it, given enough requests at once.
Hard disk... slow on both.

lines.text: Here's the lab. Read every number in an array of one gigabyte, first in order, then in a random order.
Same count. Same RAM.
How much longer does each random read take?
About twenty times, on this machine.
Memory moves in sixty four byte lines. In order, one line serves eight numbers, and the processor fetches the next lines before you ask.
At random, each read uses just one number from its line, and then it stalls. But the processor overlaps several of those stalls.
Make each address depend on the last read, and nothing overlaps: a hundred and fifty eight nanoseconds, the whole D RAM wait.
Big O counted all three the same.

With k in flight, the waits overlap. So they cost about requests times alpha, divided by k.
One read from the fast drive takes eighty microseconds alone... twelve thousand five hundred reads a second.
To reach the drive's million a second... you need at least eighty in flight. Samsung measured it with a hundred and twenty eight.

lines.text: A job can't finish faster than its bytes take at bandwidth beta... or its waits take with k in flight. The floor is the larger.
One terabyte, read in order from the fast drive: a hundred and sixty two seconds moving bytes, five seconds of delay. Bandwidth bound.
The orders table, at random from a hard disk: twenty nine seconds of bytes, five thousand nine hundred fifty two of delay, at a floor of six thousandths of a second each. Latency bound.
A floor ignores everything else. So a real run is slower.

Each request also streams sixteen megabytes, so a real run needs more... Measure the rate per request before you promise it.

Thirteen seconds. A chain runs at its slowest link.
